Consult Summary:
- 48-year-old man with 3 days of frequent diarrhea, crampy lower abdominal pain, and one episode of vomiting; clinical picture most consistent with acute gastroenteritis. Supportive care advised; monitor and seek in-person review if worsening or not improving.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline:
  - Acute diarrhea for ~3 days with urgency/feeling need to go again; cannot work, needs to stay near a toilet.
  - Abdominal pain centered below the umbilicus; improves somewhat after bowel movements; audible stomach noises.
  - Nausea with one vomiting episode this morning after eating fruit; no hematemesis (red color attributed to strawberries).
  - No visible blood in stool.
  - No clear fever reported; some sweating; uncertain about temperature.
  - Possibly suboptimal fluid intake; eating seems to worsen urgency, so patient is eating lightly.
- Pertinent negatives/other ROS:
  - No chest pain.
  - Breathing at asthma baseline (uses inhaler as needed); no new respiratory symptoms.
  - Able to walk and talk; staying home due to toilet needs.
- Past medical history:
  - Asthma.
- Allergies:
  - NKDA.
- Medications:
  - Asthma inhaler; recent change in brand.
- Family history:
  - Father died of bowel (colorectal) cancer ~10 years ago.
- Social/preventive:
  - Employed; currently at home due to symptoms. Travel, sick contacts, recent antibiotics not discussed.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not available.
- Observed/reported:
  - Self-reported mild abdominal tenderness on palpation in infra-umbilical region.
  - Patient ambulatory, speaking comfortably.
  - No signs of systemic toxicity reported.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis, likely viral.
  - Supporting: Acute 3-day onset, crampy midline abdominal pain with borborygmi, urgency/tenesmus sensation, one emesis, no blood in stool, no high fever, mild tenderness only.
- Differential diagnosis (top 2–3):
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (foodborne) – medium likelihood: similar presentation; absence of blood/high fever makes invasive bacterial causes less likely.
  - IBS-D – low to low-medium likelihood: pain relief after defecation and urgency could suggest IBS, but acute onset with vomiting favors infection.
- Colorectal cancer is unlikely for this acute presentation despite family history (no chronic change in bowel habits, bleeding, weight loss).

Plan:
- Supportive care:
  - Increase oral fluids to prevent dehydration.
  - Stay home and rest until improvement.
  - Monitor for red flags: high fever, blood in stool, severe/worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, signs of dehydration (dizziness, reduced urination), or inability to tolerate fluids.
- Medications:
  - Antibiotics not recommended; may worsen illness in typical viral gastroenteritis.
- Follow-up:
  - If symptoms worsen or do not improve over the next 1–2 days, arrange in-person GP evaluation for abdominal examination.
  - Given family history concerns, focus on current acute illness; consider discussing appropriate colorectal cancer screening with GP once recovered.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  - Vitals (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure), stool characteristics (watery/mucus), exact frequency/volume, hydration signs, sick contacts, recent travel/food exposures, recent antibiotic or healthcare exposure, full medication list, alcohol/tobacco use, baseline bowel habits, weight changes, follow-up timeframe explicitly documented by clinician.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Age/DOB inconsistency in transcript (patient states age 48; earlier DOB statements were inconsistent). DDx assumes age ~48; conflict noted.
  - Patient concern about inhaler causing diarrhea; clinician stated this is very unlikely (consistent with DDx).
● Transcript quality:
  - Several incomplete/fragmented sentences and audio dropouts; some ambiguity around fever history and age/DOB. Clinical details such as vitals and stool description not captured.
